questions.q: Name two gana/sangha polities mentioned in Buddhist texts and give the modern location of their capitals.
questions.a: Correct answer: Vajji (Vrijji) confederacy with capital at Vaishali (modern Basarh, Bihar) and the Mallas with twin capitals at Kusinara (modern Kasia, Uttar Pradesh) and Pava (modern Fazilnagar, Uttar Pradesh). The Shakyas of Kapilavastu (modern Piprahwa, Uttar Pradesh) are a third example. A wrong answer (e.g., naming Magadha or Avanti) reveals the student still conflates monarchical and non-monarchical mahajanapadas and has not memorised the basic list from the NCERT text.

questions.q: Why does the NCERT textbook call gana/sanghas “oligarchies” rather than “republics” or “democracies”?
questions.a: Correct answer: Because political participation was restricted to heads of Kshatriya clans (rajas) who claimed common ancestry; women, non-Kshatriyas, slaves, and landless labourers were excluded from the assembly (santhagara). The term “republic” (res publica) implies a broader public sphere, while “democracy” implies rule by the demos (common people) — neither fits the closed, kin-based corporate structure. A wrong answer that equates gana/sangha with modern democracy shows the student imposes anachronistic categories and misses the NCERT’s explicit caution: “oligarchy refers to a form of government where power is exercised by a group of men.”

questions.q: A Buddhist text describes the Vajji sangha’s assembly as meeting “frequently and in harmony” and making decisions by “consultation and vote.” If you were a historian, what two follow-up questions would you ask to test the reliability of this description?
questions.a: Good follow-up questions: (1) Who composed this text, when, and for what audience? (Buddhist texts were composed centuries later by monks who admired the Buddha’s own Shakya gana, so they may idealise gana polities.) (2) Does archaeological or inscriptional evidence from Vaishali (e.g., seals, fortifications) corroborate a collective administration? A student who cannot generate such source-critical questions treats the text as transparent fact rather than a constructed narrative.

questions.q: Compare the resource base of the Vajji sangha (as described in the NCERT: “rajas probably controlled resources such as land collectively”) with that of Magadha (productive alluvial soil, iron mines, elephants, river transport). Which polity had a structural advantage in sustaining a standing army, and why?
questions.a: Magadha had the structural advantage. Collective land control by Vajji rajas meant revenue was dispersed among many lineages, making centralised extraction for a standing army difficult. Magadha’s monarch could directly tax fertile rice lands, monopolise iron from Jharkhand for weapons, and use the Ganga for cheap troop movement — all managed by a salaried bureaucracy. A student who says “Vajji was richer because they had more land” misses the organisational difference: collective control ≠ centralised fiscal capacity.

questions.q: The Arthashastra (Book 11, Chapter 1) advises a king to “sow dissension among the chiefs of a gana” as a strategy to conquer it. Evaluate whether this advice reflects a genuine structural weakness of gana/sanghas or merely Kautilya’s cynical realism.
questions.a: It reflects a genuine structural weakness: gana/sanghas relied on consensus among equal clan heads; if a monarch could bribe, threaten, or persuade a few key rajas, the assembly’s unity fractured. The Buddha’s advice to the Vajjis (in the Mahaparinibbana Sutta) — “meet frequently, act in concord” — implicitly acknowledges this vulnerability. A student who dismisses it as “just Kautilya being Machiavellian” fails to see that the gana’s strength (collective leadership) was also its Achilles’ heel.

questions.q: Construct a comparative table with four rows (Sovereignty, Succession, Revenue, Military) and two columns (Monarchical Mahajanapada e.g., Magadha; Gana/Sangha e.g., Vajji) that a Class 12 student could use for last-minute revision.
questions.a: A good table shows: Sovereignty — single king vs. council of rajas; Succession — hereditary primogeniture vs. selection by assembly from clan elders; Revenue — king’s officers tax cultivators directly vs. rajas collectively control land and share surplus; Military — standing army paid from treasury vs. clan levies assembled ad hoc. A poor table merely lists “king vs. no king” without institutional detail, indicating superficial memorisation.
